title: Kalinga Edict (Major Rock Edict XIII)
published_date: 3rd c. BCE (Kalinga campaign in Ashoka's 8th regnal year, c. 262-261 BCE)

access.edition_or_version: E. Hultzsch, Inscriptions of Asoka, Major Rock Edicts (1925 ed. and trans.), Edict XIII at p. 43 — public domain (verified 2026-09-24). Inscriptions name the king 'Devanampiya Priyadasi'. Thapar's study (OUP) supplies the historical analysis.

tone_mechanisms_observed: public first-person evaluation of the ruler's own earlier conduct: conquest-mindedness, its human cost, remorse, policy revision
enumerative, additive clauses: reflection unfolds as catalogued accountability rather than lyric outburst
past-tense report of the war followed by present-tense declarations of policy — the same past-to-present structure as recollected-tranquillity reflection
reflection issues in concrete resolutions: here reflection produces action, countering 'reflection that halts plot'
mechanics.point_of_view: Public first-person of the ruler judging his own past from the standpoint of its victims — the ruler as second party to his own judgment.
mechanics.tense_and_structure: Past-tense narrative of war and aftermath opening into present-tense declarations of intent; the turn from then to now is the edict's rhetorical engine.
mechanics.rhythm_and_cadence: Solemn, measured cadence of inscriptional prose; no lyric acceleration.
mechanics.psychic_distance: Maximal self-distance by perspective-shift: an emperor recounts his war from the victims' side. (Comparable to Kross's self-distancing frame as an analytic analogy only — not historical influence.)
mechanics.style_and_devices: Sparse; the moral vocabulary of Dhamma frames reflection as obligation rather than feeling; the single dominant figure is the ruler submitted to his own reckoning.
mechanics.copyright_note: Ancient inscription public domain; Hultzsch 1925 translation public domain; Thapar's study in copyright. Paraphrased only; no inscription text reproduced.
mechanics.verification_note: The eighth-regnal-year date for the Kalinga campaign (c. 262-261 BCE) was web-verified 2026-09-24; the edict's own erection date is not firmly pinned — do not print a single firm inscription date without an epigraphic citation.
